title: The Ibadis
hookLine: the school of Oman and parts of North Africa, which rejects the Kharijite label
last: ZAYDIS SEEK AN IMAM WHO COMES FORWARD OPENLY.

cards: A nickname nobody asked for. It sticks at school, at work, in the family. It comes from an old story, or from somebody else's mistake, and the person wearing it wants to say: that's not me.
Now stretch that across a whole community and a long history. A school of Islam, rooted in Oman and in pockets of North Africa, has been handed a label in other people's books.
Its scholars have spent a long time answering, patiently: that's not us. Today, the Ibadis, and the name they refuse.

teach.h: NAMED FOR ABD ALLAH IBN IBAD.
teach.b: Tradition says the school is named for Abd Allah ibn Ibad, an early figure in Basra, and Ibadis also honor a scholar of that city, Jabir ibn Zayd, as a teacher at their root. Now the label.
In the early civil wars, a group broke away from Ali's camp.

teach.h: THE LABEL: THOSE WHO WENT OUT.
teach.b: Others called them the Khawarij, those who went out. Some of them declared other Muslims unbelievers and treated their blood as lawful. Some writers outside the school filed the Ibadis under that same heading.
Ibadi scholars answer that the extremists who killed other Muslims were wrong, and that their own teachers broke from them over exactly that.
To an Ibadi, other Muslims stay inside the faith: people to live beside, pray near and trade with. And there's a verse they can point to.

The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "neither defame one another, nor insult one another by nicknames." A label used to push someone out of the community is the kind of thing that line warns against. Last, the place.
In Oman the Ibadi school has deep roots, with its own scholars, mosques and law.
It's also found in parts of North Africa, in desert valleys and on islands, and in communities along the East African coast.

Its jurists write their own books of fiqh, with their own methods, and they can tell you exactly where they differ from their neighbors and where they agree. A school with its own name, asking to be called by it.

how: Ibadi Muslims, centered in Oman with communities in North Africa and East Africa, follow their own school of law and theology; they reject being called Kharijites and hold that other Muslims remain within the faith.

games.q: you're an Ibadi scholar, and a book written outside your school files you under the Kharijites. what do you answer?
o: accept the label and move on.
say the extremists were wrong to kill other Muslims, and that your teachers broke from them.
games.why: Ibadi scholars answer that the extremists were wrong, and that their own school parted from them over shedding Muslim blood.

practice: Say the pair once, slowly: Ibadi, Oman, and let it settle as a name, not a label.

Then think of one person you've known only by a label, a coworker, a neighbor, a group in the news, and quietly say the name they'd choose for themselves. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer.
